name: THE GORGON-BABY-GONE BURGER (comes with gorgonzola cheese)

recipe.history:
Gorgonzola is one of the world's oldest blue-veined cheeses, with a history rooted in the town of Gorgonzola in the Lombardy region of northern Italy, near Milan. Legend holds that its creation was accidental — a cheesemaker in the ninth or tenth century left fresh curd overnight and then incorporated it with the next day's batch, unknowingly creating conditions for the green-blue mold Penicillium glaucum to flourish through the combined mass. Whether this origin story is true or apocryphal, Gorgonzola has been documented as a distinct cheese since at least the eleventh century, and by the fifteenth century it was well enough established that it was traded as a valuable commodity across northern Italy. Today the cheese carries a Protected Designation of Origin (DOP) status and must be produced in specific regions of Lombardy and Piedmont. There are two main styles: Gorgonzola Dolce, young and soft, with a creamy, buttery texture and mild blue flavor, and Gorgonzola Piccante (or Naturale), firmer, more crumbly, and significantly more pungent, with intense earthy, spicy, and sharp notes that develop over a longer aging period.

Blue cheese in American cuisine occupied a narrow lane for most of the twentieth century — it was the cheese in blue cheese dressing, the classic pairing for a wedge salad at steakhouses. But the artisan cheese revolution of the late 1990s and 2000s, combined with a growing interest in Italian regional cooking, elevated Gorgonzola into the mainstream gourmet kitchen. Chefs began using it not just as a flavor accent but as a primary ingredient — in risottos, pastas, stuffed meats, and eventually on burgers. A Gorgonzola burger became a signature item at upscale casual chains and independent burger joints throughout the 2000s, often paired with sweet caramelized onions, candied walnuts, or pear to balance the cheese's boldness. The logic is the same as it is in classic cheese and fruit pairings: a sharp, pungent blue needs something sweet and approachable to serve as a bridge for the palate.

I made my first Gorgonzola burger for a dinner I was nervous about — cooking for someone I wanted to impress and whose food opinions I respected more than my own at the time. I had decided on burgers because they are forgiving, and I had decided on Gorgonzola because I thought it would signal sophistication without trying too hard. What I didn't anticipate was how perfectly the cheese would work: I crumbled Gorgonzola Dolce over the patty in the last minute of cooking, put a lid on the pan to trap steam, and watched through the glass as the cheese softened and pooled into the crevices of the crust like something that had always belonged there. The dinner went well. The burger was remembered and requested again months later by name. I have made it many times since, and it has never disappointed, partly because Gorgonzola is nearly impossible to use badly, and partly because I have learned — through this recipe and others — to trust bold ingredients to do what they do.

Medium rare is the only internal temperature for a burger in this kitchen: 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, 54 to 57 degrees Celsius. I feel this conviction most strongly with Gorgonzola burgers because the cheese is so assertive, so loaded with flavor, that an overcooked dry patty simply cannot stand up to it. A well-done burger under Gorgonzola tastes like the cheese is bullying the meat. A medium-rare burger under Gorgonzola tastes like a partnership — the beef's richness and the mineral, slightly funky depth of the cheese finding each other in the middle, neither one dominating. The pink, juicy center of a properly cooked patty has enough flavor and enough fat to hold its own against even Gorgonzola Piccante. That is the balance I am always looking for, and medium rare is the only way to find it.
ingredients: 1/3 cup walnuts, toasted and finely chopped
1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
6 oz Gorgonzola Dolce (or half Dolce, half Piccante for more intensity)
2 ripe but firm Bosc pears, peeled, cored, and sliced 1/4 inch thick
instructions: 1. Make the caramelized onion jam: Heat butter and olive oil in a wide skillet over medium-low heat. Add onions and a pinch of salt. Cook 40–50 minutes, stirring occasionally, until very soft and golden. Add balsamic vinegar and brown sugar, stir well, and cook 10 more minutes until jammy. Season with pepper. Set aside.

2. Make the candied walnuts: Melt butter in a small skillet over medium heat. Add sugar and stir until it begins to dissolve. Add walnuts, cayenne, and salt. Toss constantly for 3–4 minutes until sugar coats and caramelizes around the nuts. Pour onto a parchment-lined plate, separate the walnuts, and let cool. Break apart and set aside.

3. Make the walnut-wheat bun dough: Combine yeast, honey, warm water, and warm milk in a stand mixer bowl. Let bloom 5 minutes. Add egg, butter, salt, whole wheat flour, and bread flour. Mix with dough hook 7 minutes. Add chopped walnuts and mix 1 more minute. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and rise 1 hour.

4. Divide dough into 4 balls, shape into bun rounds on a parchment-lined sheet, cover, and proof 45 minutes. Preheat oven to 375°F. Brush with egg wash and bake 16–18 minutes until deep golden. Cool completely.

5. Make the balsamic pears: Melt butter in a skillet over medium-high heat. Add pear slices in a single layer. Sprinkle with brown sugar and cinnamon. Cook undisturbed 2 minutes until golden. Flip and cook 1 minute more. Deglaze with balsamic vinegar and toss. Season with salt. Set aside.
6. Make the Gorgonzola cream: In a small saucepan over very low heat, combine Gorgonzola and heavy cream. Stir gently until cheese melts into a pourable sauce. Keep warm.
7. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 portions (about 6 oz each). Form into patties 3/4 inch thick with a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides generously with salt and pepper.

8. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Sear patties undisturbed 3 minutes. Flip and cook 2–3 more minutes. Check internal temperature — pull at 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest 3 minutes.
9. Toast bun halves cut-side down in the skillet 60–90 seconds.

10. Assemble: Spread a generous spoonful of caramelized onion jam on the bottom bun. Add a handful of baby spinach. Place the medium-rare patty on top. Spoon warm Gorgonzola cream over the patty. Arrange balsamic pear slices on top. Scatter candied walnuts over everything. Finish with flaky sea salt and the top bun. Serve immediately.
